# Templates

A template is a stored subject and body with `{{ variable }}` placeholders.
Send one by naming its **slug** instead of passing `html`:

```ts
const { id } = await sendsprite.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: ["ada@example.com"],
  template: "welcome",
  variables: { name: "Ada" },
});
```

Over REST:

```bash
curl -X POST "https://sendsprite.com/api/v1/emails" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ss_live_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    "to": ["ada@example.com"],
    "template": "welcome",
    "variables": { "name": "Ada" }
  }'
# → 201 {"id":"em_…"}
```

The render happens on the server, and the rendered subject and bodies are what
is stored and what is sent. `template` cannot be combined with `html` or
`text` — exactly one content source — and `variables` is refused without
`template`. `subject` is optional when a template supplies one, and a
request-level `subject` overrides the template's.

Creating one is a slug, a name, a subject and an HTML body:

```ts
await sendsprite.templates.create({
  slug: "welcome",
  name: "Welcome",
  subject: "Welcome, {{ name }}",
  bodyHtml: "<p>Hi {{ name }}, thanks for signing up.</p>",
  bodyText: "Hi {{ name }}, thanks for signing up.",
  variablesSchema: { variables: [{ name: "name", type: "string" }] },
});
```

```bash
curl -X POST "https://sendsprite.com/api/v1/templates" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ss_live_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "slug": "welcome", "name": "Welcome", "subject": "Welcome, {{ name }}",
        "bodyHtml": "<p>Hi {{ name }}, thanks for signing up.</p>" }'
# → 201 {"id":"tpl_…","slug":"welcome","version":1,…}
```

A slug is lower-case letters, digits and single dashes, up to 64 characters;
a name up to 120; each body up to 5 MB. `bodyText` is optional and
`variablesSchema` defaults to no declarations. The SDK's `templates` resource
is `list()`, `iterate()`, `get(slug)`, `create()`, `update(slug, …)`,
`remove(slug)` and `render(slug, variables)` — there is no `rename()`, for
the reason under _Versioning_.

Managing templates needs a **`full`** API key, `POST /templates/:slug/render`
included, because both return template content. Sending _with_ a template does
not: a `sending_only` key calls `POST /emails` and the server renders. In the
dashboard, every team role can manage templates.

## The syntax

`{{ name }}`, and nothing else. Whitespace inside the braces is ignored, and
names may be dotted (`{{ user.firstName }}`, up to four segments) to reach into
a nested object. A name is letters, digits and underscores, starting with a
letter or an underscore.

There are **no** helpers, filters, conditionals or loops, and there is **no
unescaped form** — no `{{{ }}}`, no `| safe`. A template engine's value is its
expression language, and its expression language is its attack surface; this
renders your customers' data into HTML that is then emailed, so there is
deliberately nothing to sandbox. For anything that needs logic, render it
yourself and pass `html` (the SDK's `react` option does exactly that).

Substituted text is never re-scanned, so a value containing `{{x}}` produces
the literal `{{x}}`. Dotted lookups walk own properties only, so
`{{ a.constructor }}` resolves to nothing rather than to a function.

A single field may use at most **500 placeholder occurrences**.

## Escaping

Escaping is decided by the field, not by you:

| Field      | Rule                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `bodyHtml` | Every substituted value is HTML-escaped: `&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, `'`, and also `` ` `` and `=`.                                                          |
| `bodyText` | No escaping — it is not markup.                                                                                                                      |
| `subject`  | No HTML escaping, but the **rendered** subject is trimmed and then refused if it is empty, longer than 998 characters, or holds a control character. |

The backtick and `=` are escaped because unquoted attributes are ordinary in
hand-written email HTML: in `<a href={{u}}>`, a value of
`x onmouseover=alert(1)` becomes a real event handler without using a single
quote character. Escaping `=` is what actually closes that, because attribute
_names_ are not entity-decoded. The cost is that a literal `=` in visible text
is emitted as `&#61;`, which the mail client decodes back to `=`.

The subject rule is the one that matters most: a CR or LF in a subject is
header injection, and the check on what you _send_ cannot see what a template
_renders_, so it is repeated on the output. The rendered check covers every C0
control character and DEL, matching the rule `POST /emails` applies to a
subject you write yourself.

Three things escaping does not do, and you should know all three:

- It does not make a URL safe. `<a href="{{link}}">` with a `javascript:` value
  survives escaping. Validate URLs you interpolate.
- It does not cover `<style>` or `<script>`. CSS `url()` and `@import` need no
  HTML-special character, so a placeholder does not belong inside a style
  element; inside a script, entities are not decoded, so a value arrives
  corrupted rather than executed. Neither is a place for a placeholder.
- It does not sanitise the **template**. Whatever your team writes into
  `bodyHtml` is sent as written, exactly as `html` on `POST /emails` is.

## Variables

Every placeholder must resolve, or the send is refused with a
`validation_error` naming what is missing. A silent empty string produces
"Hi ," at volume, and you find out from a customer rather than from a test.

Values may be strings, numbers or booleans. `null`, `NaN`, objects and arrays
are refused rather than rendered. An empty or whitespace-only string counts as
**missing**, not as a value — a blank CSV cell is `""`, and mailing "Hi ,"
because of one is the failure this rule exists to prevent.

Declare a variable with a `default` to make it genuinely optional:

```json
{
  "variablesSchema": {
    "variables": [
      { "name": "name", "type": "string", "default": "there" },
      {
        "name": "credits",
        "type": "number",
        "description": "Shown in the header"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

`default` is the only way to make a placeholder optional. There is deliberately
no `required` flag: the renderer refuses every unresolved placeholder, so
`required: true` would be a no-op, and `required: false` could only mean
"render nothing here". To substitute a genuinely empty value, declare
`default: ""` — explicit rather than accidental.

A declared `type` is enforced against the supplied value at render time and
against the `default` when the template is saved; a name declared twice is
refused. A `description` is shown in the dashboard editor and nowhere else. A
template may declare up to 100 variables.

A supplied `variables` payload is bounded: at most **200 keys** (counting
nested objects and array items), **2 000 characters** per value, and **64 KB**
serialised. Per-recipient content larger than that is what the `html` field is
for.

## Versioning

Every content change bumps `version` and appends a snapshot.
`GET /api/v1/templates/:slug` returns the 20 most recent versions alongside the
template, and **Restore** in the dashboard applies an old snapshot as a _new_
version — history is append-only, so what was live and when stays readable, and
a restore is itself undoable. An update that changes nothing bumps nothing.

Every `:slug` route also accepts the `tpl_…` id — the two cannot collide,
because a slug admits neither an underscore nor an upper-case letter — so
`sendsprite.templates.get(created.id)` works straight after a `create()`.

`slug` cannot be changed; `PATCH` does not accept the field. A live send names a
template by slug, so a rename would be a silent outage — create the new one and
delete the old.

Deleting a template leaves the emails it produced alone: their stored bodies
stay exactly as they were sent, and the link back to the template becomes
`null`.

## Writing one: blocks or HTML

The dashboard offers two ways to author a body, and a template remembers which
one it was written with.

**Design** is the same visual editor campaigns use — a palette of blocks,
drag-and-drop, columns, and a style panel for the selection. It is what a new
template opens in. Placeholders work exactly as they do anywhere else: type
`{{ name }}` into a heading or a paragraph.

**HTML** is a textarea. It is what you want for markup you already have, for
anything the block set does not cover, and for a template that a designer
hands you as a file.

Switching **Design to HTML** keeps the markup the blocks currently produce and
turns the visual editor off for that template — a design that no longer
produces the stored HTML would overwrite your next hand edit, so it is
discarded rather than kept. Switching **HTML to Design** cannot parse arbitrary
markup back into blocks, so it starts a new body; the editor says so before it
does anything.

None of this changes the API. `body_html` is what is stored and what is sent,
`POST /templates` still takes HTML, `templates pull` still writes an
`.html` file, and a template created through the API simply has no design and
opens in HTML mode. The block tree is the dashboard editor's own source and is
not part of the REST contract.

One difference worth knowing: a template body carries **no unsubscribe
footer**, whichever way it was written. Campaigns are bulk mail to a list and
always append one; a template is the body of a transactional send, and a
password reset with an unsubscribe link under it is not a thing anyone wants.

A template built in Design mode carries a **theme** too — the page and card
colours, the width, the font — stored beside the blocks and compiled into
`body_html` on every save. As with campaigns, an absent theme is the renderer's
defaults, and neither the theme nor the block tree appears in the REST
response: the API deals in HTML.

## Sending yourself a test

**Send a test** on a saved template mails one copy through the ordinary send
path, rendered from the stored row with each variable's declared default. It
is a real send: it counts against the team's limits, appears in the mail log
tagged `sendsprite_test`, and — in the SES sandbox — only arrives if the
recipient address is verified in AWS. Its subject is prefixed with `[Test]` so
it cannot be mistaken for the real thing in an inbox.

The button is disabled while there are unsaved changes, because the test
renders the template the server holds, not the one on your screen.

## Previewing

```ts
const { subject, html, text } = await sendsprite.templates.render("welcome", {
  name: "Ada",
});
```

Over REST, `POST /api/v1/templates/:slug/render` with `{ "variables": { … } }`
returns `{ subject, html, text }` without sending or storing anything. It runs
the same renderer the send path runs, so the preview cannot differ from the
send. The variables are not echoed back, and the same payload bounds apply
(the request body itself is capped at 256 KB). `text` is `null` for a
template with no text body.

The dashboard editor calls the same function in your browser, which is why its
preview updates as you type. A variable with a declared default previews with
that default; one without gets a visible stand-in — `{name}` for a string, `0`
for a number, `true` for a boolean — so you can see where the value will land.
The preview renders inside a sandboxed iframe.

## From the CLI

```bash
sendsprite templates pull ./emails    # write every template to ./emails
sendsprite templates push ./emails    # create what is missing, update the rest
sendsprite templates push ./emails --dry-run
```

The directory is flat, three files per template, named by the slug:

| File          | Holds                                               |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `<slug>.json` | `name`, `subject`, `variablesSchema`                |
| `<slug>.html` | `bodyHtml`                                          |
| `<slug>.txt`  | `bodyText` — present only when the template has one |

The slug is the identity: it is immutable server-side and already restricted to
lower-case letters, digits and dashes, so the file name carries it and no
manifest field repeats it.

Two behaviours here are safety properties rather than incidentals:

- **`push` never deletes a remote template.** A template on the instance with no
  file in the directory is reported and left alone. Deleting is explicit:
  the dashboard, or `DELETE /api/v1/templates/:slug`.
- **A missing `<slug>.txt` means "no opinion", not "clear the text body".** An
  absent file is ambiguous — never pulled, gitignored, lost — so `push` reports
  it and leaves the stored text body as it is. There is currently no CLI path to
  remove a text body; use the dashboard.

Add a `.gitattributes` to the directory:

```
* text=auto eol=lf
```

On Windows with `core.autocrlf=true` a checked-out body becomes CRLF, and `push`
will correctly — but confusingly — see that as a change to every template.
